title: A "longest log wins" vote rule lets a Raft leader overwrite committed entries
summary: Raft's election restriction compares the last log entry's term first and its index second. A developer rewrites it the intuitive way round: the candidate with more entries has seen more history, so index first, term to break ties. Every unit test passes. The prover finds a voter and a candidate for which the old rule refuses the vote and the new one grants it, which is the configuration in which a leader can overwrite an entry the cluster already committed.

change.description: Rewrite the up-to-date check so that it reads naturally: a candidate whose log is longer is more up to date, and between logs of the same length the newer last term wins. The reviewer agreed that this is "the same thing, said the other way round".

risk: The order of the comparison is the whole safety argument of Raft's leader election (section 5.4.1 of the paper). A committed entry is on a majority of servers, and any candidate that can win an election needs votes from a majority, so the two sets overlap; the term-first comparison guarantees that the overlapping voter refuses a candidate whose log lacks the committed entry. With index first, a server that was partitioned away and kept appending uncommitted entries in an old term has the longest log in the cluster, wins the election, and its new leadership overwrites entries that clients were told are committed. Data that was acknowledged is lost, silently, and only after a specific partition and a specific election, which is why such bugs reach production.
explanation: Both versions of `grant` are compiled into one program and JBMC is asked whether an input exists on which they differ. The method has eight parameters, six of them 64-bit, so the input space has 2^448 points; the solver reasons about the comparisons symbolically and answers in seconds. The witness it produces, replayed through both versions, is a voter whose last entry has a higher term than the candidate's and a candidate with a longer log: the old rule says no, the new one says yes. That input is exactly the partitioned-server scenario from the paper's figure 8. No test in the suite had it, because the suite tests the rule's clauses one at a time and this input needs two of them to disagree.
resolution: Keep term first. If the comparison must read differently, write it as a tuple comparison `(term, index)` and let the prover confirm it is the same function: a refactor that really is equivalent passes this check with no declaration, as example 017 shows for another kernel.
notes: A vote rule rewritten as "longest log wins" elects a leader that overwrites committed entries.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets 4 gaps in what the proof reaches: `class-initializer:net.terminalvalue.quorum.raft.Ballot.<clinit>()V` (both versions, first at net.terminalvalue.quorum.raft.VoteRule.grant:63); `class-initializer:net.terminalvalue.quorum.raft.LogOrder.<clinit>()V` (both versions, first at net.terminalvalue.quorum.raft.VoteRule.grant:65); `class-initializer:net.terminalvalue.quorum.raft.TermOrder.<clinit>()V` (both versions, first at net.terminalvalue.quorum.raft.VoteRule.grant:62); `class-initializer:net.terminalvalue.quorum.raft.VoteEffect.<clinit>()V` (both versions, first at net.terminalvalue.quorum.raft.VoteRule.decide:47). Under strict mode each is refused by name, and a run by the tool's own checker would end with no verdict; the example runs in `assume` until the user decides how the recorded examples move. The recorded proof is JBMC's, which strict mode of the tool's own checker does not change; the checker refuses part of it in any mode (a static JDK method it does not model (java.util.List.of(java.lang.Object[]), and 1 more); arrays of references (a new array of references); reads a static field that is not a compile-time constant (net.terminalvalue.quorum.raft.TermOrder.OLDER, and 14 more)). JBMC's own approximations are step 4c's.
provenance: Constructed from the election restriction of the Raft paper, by swapping the two components of the comparison.

references.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (section 5.4.1, election restriction)
